## 1. Intro

- A classic family of problems: top K YouTube videos, Spotify songs, many variants
- Topics: stream processing, approximation, count-min sketch, time-series databases
- Goal: build a toolkit and intuition, not memorize an answer
  - Real interviews take different trajectories
- Framework: requirements (spend real time here) → core entities → API → (no data flow) → HLD (minimal, working) → deep dives
  - Easier to optimize a working system than make an optimal one work

## 2. Functional requirements: windows matter

- "The requirements are complete, let me go" is wrong
  - Small requirement changes imply very different designs
  - Candidates fail by applying a solution built for different requirements
- **Top K most viewed videos**
- **Time windows**: all-time is boring (Gangnam Style, a Justin Bieber video); add last **hour, day, week, month**
- **Tumbling vs sliding windows**
  - Tumbling: fixed boundaries, full duration ("last week" = Sunday to Sunday)
  - Sliding: the last 7 days from now; moves forward continuously
- Strategy: assume the simple version and confirm
  - "I'll use tumbling windows; last month = month start to end; OK?"
  - Week = 7 days, month = 28 days; no calendar support
- Below the line: **arbitrary windows** (e.g., October 2019): a general analytics problem, less interesting
- Don't over-enumerate below-the-line items; keep moving
- Write-up: K capped at **1,000** (write-up)

## 3. Non-functional requirements

- Useful NFRs over comprehensive ones; don't produce one per category
- **Write-side latency: ≤ 1 minute** from view to being counted
  - Distributed systems delay and reorder events (retries, congestion, packet loss)
  - Sets an **upper bound on cache TTLs** (a 2-min TTL would violate it)
  - Lets us **ignore events arriving > 1 min late** ("lost and put on a truck")
- **Read latency: tens of ms**
  - Buckets: cache hits = single-digit ms (gold standard); well-tuned APIs = tens of ms (P99 maybe hundreds); search/LLM = hundreds of ms to minutes
  - Tells us we need precompute or caching
- **Scale**
  - **Cardinality** (number of unique items): billions of videos (TBD, refine later); can't sort that live
  - **Write volume**: hundreds of thousands of views/s (TBD; ask or estimate)
- **No approximation: precise results**
  - Precise is easier than a well-built approximate system; most interviewers don't expect count-min sketch, especially junior
- Ask: "anything else I need to cover, or can I start?"

## 4. Core entities and API

- Entities: **Video**, **View**, **Time window**
  - Not very interesting for infra problems; don't spend long
- API

```
GET /views/top?window={hour|day|month|all}&k=  -> [{ videoId: string, views: int }]
```

- Clients assume the list is sorted
- No pagination needed: K ≤ 1,000, a few KB
- Senior candidates skip quickly through uninteresting parts

## 5. HLD: all-time top K

- Shortcut: assume a **video views Kafka topic** already exists (another YouTube service writes it)
  - We're designing Top K, not YouTube
  - Big event topics are common in event-driven architectures
- **View consumer** reads the topic (scale out later; topic partitioned)
- **Views DB**: Postgres to start; table (videoId, views)
  - Each view: insert with 1 or increment
- Read: API gateway → **Top-K service** → SQL

```sql
SELECT video_id, views FROM video_views ORDER BY views DESC LIMIT :k;
```

- Fast only with an **index on views**: the index is a sorted list; take the first K
  - Without it: scan and sort every row ("Postgres might use a heap, not sure")
- Yes, it doesn't scale; say so
  - Staff can skip basic steps; junior engineers do much better starting basic

## 6. HLD: windowed top K

- All-time sums can't separate last month from last year
- Add **timestamp truncated to the hour**: (videoId, hour, views); hourly buckets per video

```sql
SELECT video_id, SUM(views) AS v FROM video_views
WHERE hour BETWEEN :start AND :end
GROUP BY video_id ORDER BY v DESC LIMIT :k;
```

- Learn SQL if you haven't; but understanding data flow conceptually is what matters
- Index on views no longer helps; an index on timestamp only prunes rows
- Must read and aggregate every row in the window: "dog slow"
- Meets the functional requirement; note the problems for deep dives

## 7. Deep dive: read latency (cache, precompute)

- Lowest-hanging fruit first: move fast, save brain-heavy topics for later
- **Read-through cache** (Redis)
  - Key: window + truncated timestamp; value: the response
  - Hits: single-digit ms; misses: minutes or hours
  - "Russian roulette": distributed systems want **predictability**
- **Precompute with a cron** (Top-K cron) each hour → cache
  - Misses are predictable: a new "last hour" every hour
- If the cron fails, don't let the service query the DB itself
  - One cron request/hour becomes thousands or millions of simultaneous DB queries
  - If the DB was the reason the cron failed, it gets much worse
- Instead: keep old entries (long TTL, e.g., 30 days); fall back to the previous window
  - Violates the 1-minute NFR, but a far better failure mode
- Write-up labels: cache top K per window (good); precompute per window (great) (write-up)

## 8. Deep dive: write volume (numbers, sharding)

- Estimates should justify decisions, not show mental arithmetic
  - Companies testing arithmetic as a job condition "suck"
- Interviewer gives: **70B views/day** (write-up: YouTube Shorts)
  - Per second: divide by ~100K (actual 86.4K) → **700K writes/s**
  - Postgres: maybe ~10K writes/s; 700K won't work
- Table size
  - **4B videos** × (8 B id + 8 B views) = 16 B → **64 GB** per full table
  - Big for many engineers, small for data systems (multi-TB NVMe)
  - But one per hour: ×24 per day
  - **Sparse**: most videos get zero views in an hour; 64 GB is an upper bound per partition
- Kafka handles 700K tiny messages/s easily; scales out
- **Partition/shard first**
  - Topic partitioned by videoId
  - View consumers own subsets of partitions
  - **Shard Postgres by videoId**: at ~10K writes/s → **~70 shards**, ~70 consumers
- Querying shards: ask each for its local top 1,000, merge
  - The global top 1,000 must lie in the union of local top 1,000s
  - Cron hits 70 DBs, but each is ~70× faster; handle retries/replicas for failed shard queries

## 9. Deep dive: batching and Flink

- Next in the "scaling writes" pattern: **batching/aggregation**
- View consumer keeps an in-memory map of counts; flushes hourly
  - Writes bounded by videos-with-views-per-hour, not views
  - DB sits idle, then gets slammed at the hour (but with much less volume)
- **Failure**: lose the in-memory aggregate?
  - Kafka with retention is the source of truth; rewind to the hour start
  - But catching up needs headroom
    - Consumers sized for exactly 700K/s: never catch up
    - At 2× (1.4M/s): 1 s of backlog per 2 s; 45 min behind → 45 min to catch up → late for the next hour
- **Checkpointing**: write partial sums to S3 every ~5 min; recover from the last checkpoint + Kafka
- That pattern is so common there's a framework: **Flink** (hourly windows, built-in checkpointing, sinks for Postgres/S3/Redis)
  - Far fewer DB shards needed: Flink absorbs the views, writes hourly aggregates
- Flink caution in interviews
  - Many designs can be one big Flink job, but interviewers may not know Flink
  - They may think you're hiding complexity: "explain the checkpointing algorithm"
  - Use sparingly; Flink as streaming aggregation is a generally safe use
- Write-up subsections: sharding ingestion, batching ingestion (write-up)

## 10. Deep dive: cheap window queries (per-window aggregates)

- Monthly query cost
  - ~24 × 30 hourly partitions: **hundreds of GB** read (sparse helps)
  - Aggregate per video: **tens of GB** (less sparse over a month), unsorted
  - Sort to top K: **KB** of output
  - Huge processing for a tiny output: "cause for pause"
- Spark/Hadoop scales it out (map: sum per video; reduce: merge sorted lists), but doesn't make it more efficient
- Better: **maintain per-window tables**: hourly, **daily, monthly**
  - Flink's hourly output also increments the day and month rows: **3× writes**
  - Each table indexed on (timestamp, views): a B-tree lookup gives top K for a period
  - Top-K cron becomes near constant time
- Correction in the video: also keep an **all-time table** (no timestamp, index on views)
- Could Flink do day/month windows and even sort to Redis, dropping the cron and Postgres?
  - Possible; but interviewers don't want "one giant Flink box," or will probe every operator
- Write-up labels: coarser granularity (good); aggregates per window in DB (great); Flink in memory (great, with caveats) (write-up)
- Junior through senior: hitting many of these points is "a pretty good spot"
- Staff extras
  - Change the rules: more windows, more topics, sliding windows
  - Ugly cases: one shard has a timestamp's views, another doesn't; how to detect and tell clients
  - Out-of-order events; how to timestamp events entering aggregation

## 11. Variant: sliding windows

- A 1-minute slide means 60 windows per hour instead of 1; worse for monthly windows
- Intuition: new window = last window + newest minute − minute that fell out
  - E.g., +6 −5 = +1
- Design
  - **Minute-grain table**: (videoId, minute, views)
  - Tables for **last hour / day / month** (no timestamp; current value), plus all-time; index on views
  - Each minute, Flink flushes minute counts; then for each window: add new minute, subtract the expired minute, apply the delta
  - Top-K cron runs **every minute**; cache key includes the minute
  - More writes; DB used as system state (unusual)
- Flink native sliding windows: a new month-long window every slide (minute) → windows × minutes per month
  - Very inefficient; could externalize state (S3, RocksDB) or build the delta approach inside Flink
- Judgment: a month-long sliding window rarely makes product sense
  - Pushing back on an interviewer's requirement is dicey; if unstated, propose sliding for hour, tumbling for month
  - Showing the cost and dialing back is "engineering maturity"

## 12. Variant: approximation (count-min sketch)

- Why: Top K likely feeds trending or a recommendation candidate generator; secondary; should be cheap
  - Rule of thumb: who notices if it's wrong, and do they care? Probably not here
- Strategically risky in interviews (more complex); a way to show off with extra time
- **Count-min sketch** ("like a Bloom filter for counts")
  - Rows = hash functions (or one hash with salts/bit slices); columns = width
  - **Add**: each row hashes the ID to a column and increments it
  - **Query**: hash to each row's cell; take the **minimum**
  - Collisions only inflate counts: the result is an **upper bound**; error depends on width and depth
  - Demo: a viewer-built simulator (adding foo twice, bar once; querying hello → 0, foo → 2)
- The sketch forgets IDs, so pair it with a **sorted set or heap** of a few thousand candidates
  - On each view: increment, query the estimate, update the sorted set if above its minimum
- **Redis**: native CMS (`CMS.INCRBY`, query) + sorted sets (`ZADD`)
  - Volatile: replicas, AOF; recovery is fuzzy, but it's an approximation anyway
- **Flink**: CMS in managed, checkpointed state; heap in memory; flush periodically to Redis
  - All in memory, lightning fast, minimal hardware; but needs Flink depth
- Sliding windows: CMS has no subtract in general, but **turnstile** updates (only removing what you added) keep guarantees
  - Remove views after 60 minutes / 1 month (separate consumer group, or Flink state)
  - Oversize the heap (e.g., 5,000) for items moving into the top K
- If an interviewer expects this, they're checking if you studied the problem; "I think it's esoteric"
  - Some users' interviewers didn't understand it: prefer simpler, proven designs

## 13. Specialized databases

- Risk: the interviewer doesn't know the technology
  - They ban it, or ask for internals; which sounds like the general solution anyway
- **TimescaleDB** (Postgres extension)
  - Hypertables for time series; **continuous aggregates** build indexed aggregate tables as data arrives
  - Fits tumbling windows well; being Postgres helps
- **Prometheus, InfluxDB**: built for single series over time (observability)
  - Top K needs sorting across billions of series (labels): effectively a scan per series
  - Write-up: can't handle that cardinality (write-up)
- **Real-time OLAP** (Druid, Pinot, ClickHouse): materialized views do the aggregation
  - Makes the problem "trivial": just config; little to discuss; interviewers may not know all three
- Advice: learn data flows and core patterns (aggregation, caching), not niche tech
- Write-up labels: InfluxDB/Prometheus (bad); TimescaleDB (good); real-time OLAP (good) (write-up)

## 14. Wrap-up and levels

- Some of this is beyond what interviews need; revisit the core deep dives
- **Understanding data flow is the unlock for infra interviews**: table sizes, where data flows, when compute happens, caching
- Write-up bars (write-up)
  - Mid-level: end-to-end, likely not optimal; finds and fixes some pinch points
  - Senior: near-optimal; finds most bottlenecks proactively; weighs technologies
  - Staff: covers unlisted deep dives; sees the whole solution space

## 15. Board as text (assembled from the talk)

```
Video views Kafka (partitioned by videoId, retention)
      |
   Flink (hourly windows, checkpoints)   [or view consumers + in-memory batch]
      |  writes hour + day + month (+ all-time) rows
      v
   Views DB (Postgres, sharded by videoId; index (timestamp, views))
      ^
   Top-K cron (hourly; per-shard top K, merge) -> Redis cache (long TTL fallback)
      ^
   API GW -> Top-K service (tens of ms)
```

- Variants: minute table + delta updates for sliding windows; Redis/Flink count-min sketch + heap for approximation
